items.title: AI Inventorship in Patent Law: Comparative Doctrine, Regulatory Divergence, and Harmonized Reform
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in invention workflows, yet patent systems continue to define inventorship in human terms. The central problem is not whether AI contributes to technical creativity, but whether existing legal doctrines can allocate ownership, responsibility, and evidentiary accountability when inventive processes are distributed across humans and AI systems. Prior scholarship has examined DABUS disputes and personhood debates, but the literature remains fragmented across jurisdictions and often under-specifies operational reform pathways for patent offices and courts. This article addresses that gap through a comparative doctrinal design covering the United States, United Kingdom, European Union/Germany, Australia, South Africa, India, China, and selected emerging jurisdictions. The analysis triangulates statutes, judicial decisions, patent-office guidance, and Scopus-indexed legal scholarship from 2019–2026. The findings show convergence on human-only inventorship, but persistent divergence in disclosure expectations, contribution tests, and evidentiary practices. These divergences produce transparency deficits, cross-border uncertainty, and uneven enforcement risk for multinational portfolios. The article’s original contribution is a six-part harmonized reform model that preserves human-centered inventorship while modernizing AI-contribution disclosure, contribution assessment, evidentiary protocols, interoperability standards, targeted supplementary protection for edge cases, and governance integration. The model is explicitly grounded in an accountability architecture framework that separates legal status from evidentiary governance. This framework offers a practical route to doctrinal stability and policy coherence without requiring full AI legal personhood.

items.title: AI Literacy and TVET Teaching Practice: The Mediating Role of Generative AI Competence in Southeast Nigeria
items.abstract: The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is transforming the knowledge, skills and pedagogical practices required of Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) educators. However, possessing basic AI literacy does not necessarily translate into meaningful AI-enabled teaching practice. This study investigates the relationship between AI literacy and AI-enabled teaching practice among TVET educators in South-Eastern Nigeria, with particular attention to the mediating role of generative AI competence in educator capacity building for global relevance. The study adoptes a correlational survey design and was conceptually anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, complemented by human-centered AI competency principles. A sample of 320 TVET educators was used for the analysis. Data were collected using an AI Literacy Scale, Generative AI Competence Scale and AI-Enabled Teaching Practice Scale. Descriptive statistics, Pearson Product Moment Correlation and Structural Equation Modelling were used for data analysis, while bootstrapping was used to test the mediation effect. The findings indicates positive relationships between AI literacy, generative AI competence and AI-enabled teaching practice. AI literacy significantly predicted generative AI competence, while generative AI competence significantly predicted AI-enabled teaching practice. The direct relationship between AI literacy and teaching practice remained significant but was reduced after the mediator was introduced, indicating partial mediation. The findings suggest that capacity building programmes should move beyond awareness of AI towards practical competence in prompt design, content generation, assessment, ethical use, verification and pedagogical integration. The study concludes that strengthening GenAI competence may constitute an important mechanism through which AI literacy is converted into meaningful teaching practice among TVET educators in South-Eastern Nigeria.

items.abstract: This paper presents an educational intervention of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted co-creative multimodal storytelling, implemented in the English course with 48 sixth-grade students at a public primary school. Students composed short descriptive paragraphs about imaginary creatures, received narrative expansions of their texts from an AI tool, and created multimodal artworks that incorporated words and phrases from these expansions. The evaluation of the intervention was based on structured observation, organized around four dimensions of motivation. The records indicate increased engagement and creative initiative, more intensive peer collaboration and the spontaneous use of new descriptive vocabulary in students' multimodal products and oral presentations. As no assessment of written production was conducted before and after the intervention, the findings are limited to observed engagement and language use.

items.title: AI-assisted peer review: efficiency for reviewers, burden for authors—a narrative review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in scholarly peer review has the potential to simplify the work of editors and reviewers through faster triage, automated reporting completeness checks, and scalable synthesis of reviewer comments. However, it also presents practical, ethical, and technical limitations that may place implementation burdens on authors. I examine bias arising from training data and model architecture, confidentiality risks from commercial AI deployment, accountability gaps when human judgment is displaced, and the growing threat of hallucinated citations to scientific integrity. I further analyze how poorly governed AI integration shifts remediation and formatting burdens onto authors—particularly those from under-resourced or non-Western institutions. I propose hybrid human–AI workflows, mandatory disclosure standards, and equity-conscious implementation frameworks to address these harms. Responsible AI integration in peer review requires transparency, human accountability, and deliberate protection of the diversity of voices represented in scientific literature. These considerations also extend beyond individual actors to recursive feedback loops in which AI-assisted manuscripts are evaluated by AI-assisted review systems, reinforcing the need for human contextual stewardship.

items.title: AI-Assisted Structural Testing Education: Test Design and Evidence-Based Interpretation
items.abstract: This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted redesign of the Civil Engineering Structural Testing Technology course, with the development of disciplinary judgment as its central objective. The redesign addresses three problems: difficulty applying knowledge learned in separate chapters to specific test decisions, insufficient verification of parameter choices and loading arrangements in student-designed test plans, and a lack of observational evidence to support the interpretation of measured data. In theoretical instruction, knowledge and reference materials are organized around relationships among test decisions; AI assists with organization and retrieval, while instructors and students jointly check the applicability of relevant standard provisions. The open-topic design assignment follows an iterative sequence of initial drafting, AI questioning, student verification, and instructor review, introducing verification before implementation. Laboratory preparation, discussion, and reporting are organized around observational evidence so that interpretations can be traced to original records. Two cases are presented: the design of a shear test for a simply supported concrete beam and an investigation of the static and dynamic characteristics of a uniform-strength cantilever steel beam. The cases examine material parameter selection and the conditions for uniform strength, respectively, and specify AI-assisted tasks, student verification methods, and assessment criteria. The course uses general-purpose large language models accessible to students and requires no dedicated platform or additional hardware investment. Its educational effectiveness remains to be examined using evidence from implementation.

items.abstract: This literature-based review looks at how artificial intelligence, including machine learning and reinforcement learning, can help optimize logic gates and circuits in processor design. It also proposes a simple experiment using benchmark circuits and discusses the limits of the approach, such as verification, generalization, and computing cost. The review concludes that AI's benefit should be measured, not assumed. items.title: AI-contextualized self-efficacy and exercise engagement among vocational college students in China: a cross-sectional serial mediation analysis of exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations
items.abstract: Background It remains unclear whether artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy, reflecting general efficacy beliefs about coping with difficulties and achieving goals with artificial intelligence support, is associated with exercise engagement. This study examined this association and specific and serial statistical indirect effects involving exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations. Methods A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted among 2,279 students recruited by convenience sampling from one vocational college in China. Participants completed self-report measures of artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy, exercise self-efficacy, exercise outcome expectations, and exercise engagement. Confirmatory factor analysis examined the measurement model. PROCESS Models 4 (preliminary) and 6 (primary) evaluated indirect effects using 5,000 bootstrap resamples and percentile 95% confidence intervals. Supplementary latent-variable structural equation models examined the theory-specified mediator ordering and its reversal. All regression and structural models adjusted for gender, age, and grade. Results In the main PROCESS analyses, artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy was positively associated with exercise engagement in the total-association model ( β = 0.427, p < 0.001). After including exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations, the direct association remained significant ( β = 0.246, p < 0.001). The specific indirect effects through exercise self-efficacy ( B = 0.047, 95% confidence interval [0.0352, 0.0598]) and exercise outcome expectations ( B = 0.048, 95% confidence interval [0.0378, 0.0586]) were significant. The serial indirect effect through exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations in the theory-specified order was also significant ( B = 0.016, 95% confidence interval [0.0116, 0.0198]). Supplementary models yielded identical fit for the two mediator orderings. Conclusion In this convenience sample, artificial intelligence-contextualized self-efficacy was associated with self-reported exercise engagement, with statistical indirect effects involving exercise self-efficacy and exercise outcome expectations. These minimally adjusted cross-sectional findings do not establish temporal ordering, causal mechanisms, or effects of actual artificial intelligence use.

items.title: AI-Driven Job Redesign in Hybrid Work
items.abstract: AI is increasingly embedded within organizational resource management, reshaping how work is designed, coordinated, evaluated, and governed. Rather than functioning solely as an automation technology, AI operates as a socio-technical actor that redistributes cognition, restructures authority, and transforms organizational control mechanisms, within hybrid work environments. This chapter develops an integrative framework for understanding AI-driven job redesign through the lenses of socio-technical systems theory, work design theory, algorithmic management, and organizational adaptation perspectives. It establishes theoretical foundations explaining how AI reconfigures work structures and human-technology relationships. It then examines how AI-driven redesign materializes operationally in hybrid contexts through algorithmic coordination, performance infrastructures, and evolving skill configurations. The analysis further explores algorithmic management as an emerging form of organizational control, highlighting tensions between efficiency, autonomy, and governance legitimacy.

items.title: AI-Driven Pharmacovigilance: New Strategies for Detecting and Monitoring Adverse Drug Reactions
items.abstract: Pharmacovigilance plays an important role in identifying, evaluating, and monitoring adverse drug reactions throughout the life cycle of medicines. Traditional pharmacovigilance systems depend mainly on spontaneous reports, clinical records, regulatory databases, and other safety information. The growing volume and complexity of these data have created a need for faster and more systematic methods of safety monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being increasingly studied for this purpose. Machine learning, natural language processing, deep learning, and other AI techniques contribute in the detection of safety signals from structured and unstructured data sources. These methods assist in analysing adverse event reports, electronic health records, clinical data, social media content, and patient-generated information. AI can also improve signal prioritization, adverse drug reaction classification, causality assessment, and prediction of potential drug-related risks. This review discusses the emerging applications of AI in pharmacovigilance, with emphasis on adverse drug reaction detection and post-marketing safety monitoring. Recent advances in transformer-based language models and real-world data integration have expanded the potential applications of AI across pharmacovigilance workflows. Even after these advancements, successful implementation depends on high-quality data, external validation, explainable AI, and continued human oversight. Future research should focus on robust clinical validation and responsible regulatory integration to ensure safe and reliable AI-assisted pharmacovigilance.
